metadata.description:
Kim Guzman: Learn to Bind off in Tunisian crochet at the end of your project.See my channel for the right-handed view. 

Subscribe to my channel for updates. 
For more information on my books and patterns: https://crochetkim.com 
Join me on Facebook: https://www.facebook.com/CrochetKim.KimGuzman/ 
Twitter: https://twitter.com/CrochetKim 
Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/crochetkimdotcom/

summary.brief: Tutorial on binding off the top edge of a Tunisian‑crochet piece.
summary.detailed: The video opens with title graphics that introduce Tunisian crochet and the binding‑off technique. The presenter explains that after completing the last row of a Tunisian‑crochet project the top edge remains open and a binding‑off row is required to close it. She first demonstrates the standard slip‑stitch bind‑off: inserting the crochet hook into a stitch, yarn‑over, pulling a loop through the stitch, and then pulling that loop through the loop already on the hook, repeating this across the row until the edge is sealed. She then shows a modified slip‑stitch bind‑off performed under the front vertical bar and the top of each stitch for a neater finish. The presenter notes that the same method works when the pattern is worked in stitch‑pattern form and encourages experimenting with different bind‑off styles. She demonstrates alternatives such as single crochet, chain‑one single crochet, double crochet, treble crochet, and shell stitches, showing a few examples. Throughout the demonstration her hands manipulate the blue yarn and crochet hook while the workpiece is held steady. The segment ends with closing graphics displaying the website address and copyright information.

action.detailed: Insert the crochet hook into each stitch of the final row, yarn‑over, pull a loop through the stitch, then pull that loop through the loop on the hook, and repeat across the row to close the top of the piece.

summary.brief: A close‑up tutorial shows a woman binding off a Tunisian crochet piece with a wooden hook and blue yarn.
summary.detailed: The video opens with a title card that reads “Tunisian Crochet – Binding Off.” The camera then cuts to a close‑up of the instructor’s hands: the left hand holds the edge of a blue‑yarn fabric while the right hand grips a wooden crochet hook, a silver ring visible on her right hand. She explains that after the last row of a Tunisian crochet project the top edge remains open, so a bind‑off row is needed to close it. First she demonstrates the standard slip‑stitch bind‑off by inserting the hook as for a slip stitch, yarning over, pulling a loop through the stitch, and then pulling that loop through the loop on the hook, repeating this across the whole row. She then shows a “modified simple stitch” bind‑off, pulling the yarn under the front vertical bar and the top of the stitch before yarning over and pulling the loop all the way through, noting that this gives a neater finish at the top. She mentions that a pattern may call for a bind‑off in the stitch pattern and that any stitch—single crochet, double crochet, treble, shells, etc.—can be used instead of a slip stitch, demonstrating a few examples. After the final loop is pulled through she cuts the yarn, pulls the end through the last loop, and weaves it in, showing how the open top becomes filled in. The segment ends with copyright slides displaying the website www.kimguzman.com and the © 2013 Kim Guzman notice.

action.detailed: Insert the wooden hook into the edge of the fabric, yarn over, pull the loop through the stitch on the hook, and repeat this slip‑stitch motion across the entire row until the top is closed, then cut the yarn and weave in the end.

summary.brief: A woman demonstrates several Tunisian‑crochet binding‑off techniques using blue yarn and a wooden hook.
summary.detailed: The tutorial opens with the instructor holding a blue Tunisian‑crochet work and a wooden hook, pointing out the open top that must be closed. She first shows the standard slip‑stitch bind‑off, inserting the hook into a stitch, yarn‑over, and pulling the loop through, repeating across the row. She then explains a modified simple‑stitch bind‑off that pulls the yarn under the front vertical bar for a neater edge, and mentions that the bind‑off can also be performed with other stitches such as single, double or treble crochet. Throughout the segment she rotates the fabric, demonstrates the motions from different angles, displays the finished edge, and a silver ring on her hand is visible. A pink wall serves as the background and a small “www.kimguzman.com” watermark appears in the corner. The close‑up view continues until the top of the piece is fully bound off and the completed edge is shown.

summary.brief: The instructor demonstrates how to bind off a finished Tunisian‑crochet piece.
summary.detailed: The video opens with the maker holding the completed Tunisian‑crochet fabric and pointing out the open top edge that needs to be closed. She first shows the standard slip‑stitch bind‑off: inserting the wooden hook into a stitch, yarn‑over, pulling a loop through the stitch on the hook, and then pulling that loop through the loop on the hook, repeating this across the row. Next she demonstrates her preferred modified slip‑stitch bind‑off, where the hook is placed under the front vertical bar and the top of each stitch, yarn‑over, and the yarn is pulled all the way through, giving a neat edge at the very top of the work. She also shows that other stitches—single crochet, double crochet, treble crochet, or decorative shell stitches—can be used in place of the slip stitch for the bind‑off. Throughout the segment she moves the yarn with her right hand, guides the hook with her left hand, rotates the work, and finishes with a smooth, closed edge before the closing credits appear.

action.detailed: Insert the hook into each stitch, yarn over, pull a loop through the stitch on the hook, then pull that loop through the loop on the hook, repeating across the row, and optionally use the modified method that goes under the front vertical bar and top of each stitch.

nodes.plm_caption:
A crochet hook and a blue stitch is being used to show and explain how to crochet. There is a ring on the right middle finger. There is a pink flat background. There are words in the lower left corner. There is a light shining in a yellow colour.
There is a wooden crochet hook in the left hand and two blue stitches in the right hand. The left hand moves the crochet hook into the stitch in the right hand and comes out, then pulls the yarn through the stitch. The right hand moves with the hook into the stitch, then twists the hook and comes out. The right hand moves back with the hook into the stitch, then into the previous stitch. The hook twists in and out of the second stitch and repeats.  The hook twists into and out of the third stitch and repeats. Then the hook twists into and out of the fourth stitch and repeats. Then the hook twists into and out of the fifth stitch and repeats. Then the hook twists into and out of the sixth stitch and repeats. Then the hook twists into and out of the seventh stitch and repeats. Then the hook twists into and out of the eighth stitch and repeats. The right hand repeats this motion for a ninth stitch and then continues onto the tenth stitch.  Once the tenth stitch is complete, the left hand turns the work counterclockwise and moves the stitches forward with the right thumb and index finger. Then the left index finger rotates the crochet stitch in a counter-clockwise motion.  The left hand repeats this motion once to the last stitch. Once the last stitch is completed, the left hand rotates the work counterclockwise with the right thumb and index finger.  The hook is pulled through all of the stitches with the right hand, and then the left hand turns the work counterclockwise again, then pushes it forward in an outward motion with the left and right index fingers. The video ends with the stitch and hook in the same place as it started.
There is light shining from the upper-right.

summary.brief: The crocheter binds off the final row of a blue Tunisian‑crochet piece.

She inserts the hook into successive stitches, pulls the yarn through, twists the hook, and repeats this motion across about ten stitches. After the tenth stitch she rotates the work counter‑clockwise, uses her thumb and index finger to pull the stitches forward, then repeats the insert‑pull‑twist sequence for the remaining stitches. Finally she pulls all remaining loops through with the hook, completing the bind‑off and returning the hook and work to their starting positions. A silver ring glints on her right middle finger, a soft yellow light shines from the upper‑right, and a small watermark appears in the lower‑left corner.

action.detailed: With the left hand holding the crochet hook, she inserts the hook into each stitch, pulls the blue yarn through, twists the hook, repeats across the row, then rotates the work counter‑clockwise, uses her thumb and index finger to bring the remaining stitches forward, and pulls all remaining loops through with the hook to finish the bind‑off.

summary.brief: A close‑up shows the woman pulling yarn through stitches with a wooden crochet hook to bind off a blue Tunisian‑crochet edge.
summary.detailed: The camera stays on the woman's hands as she holds the partially finished blue fabric in her right hand and a wooden crochet hook in her left. She inserts the hook into the next stitch, yarn‑overs, and pulls the loop through both the stitch and the hook, creating a slip‑stitch that tightens the edge. She repeats this motion, moving the hook horizontally from left to right across the row until the work is bound off. A silver ring glints on her finger throughout, a faint "www.kimguzman.com" watermark appears in the corner, and the background is a pinkish‑white surface.

action.detailed: Insert the crochet hook into the next stitch, yarn over, pull the loop through the stitch and the hook, and continue this slip‑stitch motion across the row to bind off the fabric.

nodes.plm_caption:
A close-up shot of a woman holding knitting needles and yarn. She talks while she knits.
The woman is holding knitting needles with her left hand and a yarn with her right. Her right hand also holds the yarn once she has her left index and thumb finger on the stitch she is working on. She starts by explaining something with her right index finger before pulling back and inserting her left knitting needle with yarn wrapped around it into a stitch. She then rotates the work piece counterclockwise, rotates her thumb and index finger horizontally back to face right, inserts her left needle once more into a stitch and pulls it through with the same stitch on her right needle. She continues repeating the pattern with a third stitch. She lifts her work piece to point at it with her right index finger. Finally, she uses her left thumb and index finger to turn the work piece right-side up and continues inserting the knitting needle with yarn and pulling it through stitches. She then talks with her mouth, inserts the knitting needle into a stitch and then pulls it out. She repeats this pattern once more and then rotates her work piece counterclockwise. She rotates back to face right, inserts the knitting needle once more and then pulls it through the stitch. She then rotates her work piece counterclockwise and inserts her left index finger to point out a stitch and the woman talks. She takes her left thumb and index finger to hold the knitting needle and yarn.

summary.brief: The woman demonstrates a left‑handed binding‑off for Tunisian crochet using a wooden hook and bright blue yarn.

She inserts the hook into a stitch, wraps the yarn, y‑overs, pulls the loop through both the stitch and the loop on the hook, then rotates the workpiece to keep the stitches oriented. She repeats this insertion‑yarn‑over‑pull‑through motion across several stitches, pointing out individual loops with her fingers, and continues the modified slip‑stitch binding‑off until the edge is closed. The background is a soft pink/white surface and a small “www.kimguzman.com” watermark appears in the lower corner.

action.detailed: Insert the left crochet hook into each stitch, yarn‑over, pull the loop through both the stitch and the loop on the hook, and repeat across the row to bind off the edge.

summary.brief: Hands demonstrate a modified slip‑stitch bind‑off in Tunisian crochet.
summary.detailed: The camera stays on a pale pink/white background as the crocheter’s hands work with a light‑colored wooden hook and bright blue yarn. She holds the partially finished fabric in her right hand while the left hand grips the hook. First she makes a loop of yarn around the hook, then inserts the hook under the front vertical bar of the last stitch and under the top loop of that stitch. She yarns over and pulls the yarn through both loops, creating a slip‑stitch bind‑off. This motion is repeated across the row, filling the open top edge of the piece. A small silver ring glints on her right ring finger throughout, and a faint website watermark remains in the lower‑left corner.

action.detailed: Insert the wooden crochet hook under the front vertical bar and the top loop of the previous stitch, yarn over, and pull the yarn through both loops to form a slip‑stitch bind‑off, then repeat this sequence across the row.

First she pulls the yarn through an existing loop, wraps it around the hook’s neck and slides the hook leftward, completing a slip‑stitch‑style bind‑off. summary.brief: A close‑up shows a woman crocheting with a wooden hook and blue yarn, forming double‑crochet stitches.
summary.detailed: The camera stays on the woman's hands. Her left hand holds an elongated wooden crochet hook while her right hand grips a ball of bright blue yarn that rests on her thumb. She moves the hook into a stitch of the fabric from the front, then from the back, pulling the yarn through to create a loop. She repeatedly yarn‑overs, pulls up loops, and draws the yarn through the two loops on the hook, then through the remaining two loops, completing a double‑crochet stitch. This sequence is performed several times, filling the top edge of the piece. A silver ring glints on one finger throughout the demonstration.

action.detailed: Insert the wooden hook into the stitch, yarn over, pull up a loop, yarn over again, draw the yarn through the two loops on the hook, yarn over once more, and pull through the remaining two loops to complete the double crochet.

summary.brief: The instructor binds off the edge of a blue Tunisian‑crochet piece using a hook.
summary.detailed: The camera stays on a close‑up of the woman's hands against a plain white‑pink background. She holds the partially finished blue fabric in her right hand while a wooden crochet hook rests in her left hand. She forms a new loop with the working yarn, brings the hook through that loop, then pulls the yarn through the two loops already on the hook, creating a single closed stitch. She slides the completed stitch off the hook, moves her index finger to guide the yarn, forms another loop, and repeats the pull‑through motion, continuing the modified slip‑stitch bind‑off until the top edge of the piece is sealed. A silver ring is visible on her right pinky finger, a black border runs along the bottom and left edges of the frame, and a “www.kimguzman.com” watermark appears in the lower‑left corner.

action.detailed: Use the crochet hook to pull the working yarn through the two loops on the hook, slide the new stitch off, and repeat to close the edge of the fabric.

summary.brief: The crocheter binds off the edge of the blue work using single‑crochet stitches.
summary.detailed: The hands insert the wooden hook into a stitch of the blue Tunisian‑crochet piece, yarn‑over and pull the yarn through both loops on the hook to make a single crochet stitch; this is repeated across several stitches, each time creating a new loop, and the final pull draws the last loop through the remaining loops, completing the bind‑off.

action.detailed: Insert the hook into a stitch, yarn‑over, pull the yarn through both loops on the hook to form a single crochet, repeat this across the remaining stitches, and finish by pulling the final loop through the last loops to close the edge.

summary_sent_to_llm.description:
Kim Guzman: Learn to Bind off in Tunisian crochet at the end of your project.See my channel for the right-handed view. 

Subscribe to my channel for updates. 
For more information on my books and patterns: https://crochetkim.com 
Join me on Facebook: https://www.facebook.com/CrochetKim.KimGuzman/ 
Twitter: https://twitter.com/CrochetKim 
Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/crochetkimdotcom/
summary_sent_to_llm.root_summary: The video opens with title graphics that introduce Tunisian crochet and the binding‑off technique. The presenter explains that after completing the last row of a Tunisian‑crochet project the top edge remains open and a binding‑off row is required to close it. She first demonstrates the standard slip‑stitch bind‑off: inserting the crochet hook into a stitch, yarn‑over, pulling a loop through the stitch, and then pulling that loop through the loop already on the hook, repeating this across the row until the edge is sealed. She then shows a modified slip‑stitch bind‑off performed under the front vertical bar and the top of each stitch for a neater finish. The presenter notes that the same method works when the pattern is worked in stitch‑pattern form and encourages experimenting with different bind‑off styles. She demonstrates alternatives such as single crochet, chain‑one single crochet, double crochet, treble crochet, and shell stitches, showing a few examples. Throughout the demonstration her hands manipulate the blue yarn and crochet hook while the workpiece is held steady. The segment ends with closing graphics displaying the website address and copyright information.

Bind off a row of Tunisian crochet stitches

You evaluate YouTube videos for a video-understanding benchmark.

You will be given an Action100M-style summary of one video: title, description,
a hierarchical GPT-written summary of the whole video, and a deduplicated list
of action labels extracted at multiple levels of the video.

Your job is to judge:

1) DOMAINS — does this video clearly belong to either of these target domains?
   - "kitchen": a person preparing food in a kitchen-like setting
     (cooking, baking, food prep — NOT eating reviews, NOT pet-food prep,
